common.medicalNotice: General information: it does not replace your doctor's advice.

signs.blood: A lot of blood in your stools
signs.dehydration: Signs of dehydration (intense thirst, dry mouth, very little urine, dizziness)

what.title: What is Crohn's disease?
what.text: It is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The immune system causes inflammation of the wall of the digestive tract. It is not contagious and it is not your fault.

where.title: Which parts of the body?
where.text: It can affect the whole digestive tract, from the mouth to the anus. Most often it affects the end of the small intestine (ileum) and the colon.

course.title: How does it evolve?
course.text: It alternates between flares, when symptoms are present, and periods of remission, when they ease or disappear. With regular treatment and follow-up, many patients lead an active life.

causes.title: Why me?
causes.text: The exact cause is unknown. It combines a genetic predisposition, an abnormal reaction of the immune system and environmental factors. Smoking is the best-known aggravating factor.

digestive.title: Digestive symptoms
digestive.text: Abdominal pain (often lower right), lasting diarrhoea, sometimes with blood or mucus, an urgent need to go to the toilet. Lesions around the anus (fissures, abscesses, fistulas) are possible.

general.title: General symptoms
general.text: Severe tiredness, loss of appetite, weight loss, sometimes fever. Fatigue is common, even between flares: talk about it with your care team.

extra.title: Outside the gut
extra.text: The disease can also affect the joints (pain), the skin, the eyes (redness, pain) or the liver. Report these symptoms to your doctor.

goals.title: What are treatments for?
goals.text: There is no treatment yet that cures the disease for good. Treatments aim to calm the inflammation, achieve and then maintain remission, and prevent complications.

families.title: Several families of medicines
families.text: Depending on your situation, your doctor may suggest anti-inflammatories, corticosteroids for a limited time, immunosuppressants or biologics. The choice and the dose are personal: your doctor decides them.

surgery.title: What about surgery?
surgery.text: Surgery is sometimes needed, for example for a narrowing of the bowel or a complication. It does not cure the disease but can bring a lot of relief. It is discussed with the medical team.

adherence.title: Taking your treatment well
adherence.text: Keep taking your treatment even when you feel well: that is what helps prevent flares. Never stop or change a medicine without your doctor's advice. CronCare reminders are there to help.

followup.title: Regular follow-up
followup.text: Consultations, blood tests and examinations help adjust your treatment. Write your symptoms in the journal to discuss them with your doctor. Check your vaccinations with your doctor, especially before some treatments.

food.title: Food
food.text: There is no single diet. During a flare, adapted eating can help; in remission, eat as varied as possible. Ask your doctor or a dietitian for advice. See also the Recipes section.

activity.title: Physical activity
activity.text: Gentle, regular activity (walking, swimming, cycling…) helps against fatigue and stress. Adapt the effort to how you feel and rest during flares.

mind.title: Your wellbeing matters
mind.text: Living with a chronic disease can be hard. Talking to your loved ones, your care team, a psychologist or other patients in the Community can help.

menstruation.title: During your period
menstruation.text: Many women notice more abdominal pain or diarrhoea just before or during their period. This is common and is not necessarily a flare.

contraception.title: Contraception
contraception.text: Some medicines and some forms of the disease can influence the choice of contraception. Discuss it with your gastroenterologist and gynaecologist.

pregnancy.title: Planning a pregnancy
pregnancy.text: Pregnancy is usually possible. It is best planned with your doctors, ideally during remission. Do not stop your treatment on your own if you are pregnant: talk to your doctor first.

journal.title: Tip
journal.text: Write your symptoms in the journal and note your period days: it will help your doctor tell the difference with a flare.

why.title: Why it matters
why.text: In people with Crohn's disease, smoking increases the risk of flares, complications and surgery, and can make treatments less effective.

benefits.title: It is never too late
benefits.text: Quitting helps at any stage of the disease. The benefits on the disease build up gradually in the months after quitting.

shisha.title: What about shisha?
shisha.text: Shisha (hookah) also contains tobacco and produces a lot of smoke: it is not a less harmful alternative to cigarettes.

help.title: Get support
help.text: Your doctor or a smoking-cessation specialist can support you and offer suitable help. Being supported greatly increases your chances of success.

meds.readOnly: Your treatment is prescribed by your doctor. To change anything, talk to them.

flareOften.title: During a flare: often better tolerated
flareOften.text: Cooked, low-fibre foods: white rice, pasta, potatoes, cooked and peeled carrots and courgettes, white meat, fish, eggs, stewed fruit. Everyone reacts differently: notice what suits you.

flareLimit.title: During a flare: often best limited
flareLimit.text: Raw vegetables, pulses (chickpeas, lentils), fruit with skin or seeds, very fatty, fried or very spicy food (harissa), fizzy drinks. This advice is temporary and should be adapted with your doctor.

remission.title: In remission
remission.text: Eat as varied as possible to avoid deficiencies. Reintroduce foods gradually, one at a time. A very restrictive diet is not recommended without medical advice.

hydration.title: Stay hydrated
hydration.text: Drink water regularly, especially with diarrhoea or in hot weather. Soups and broths also help replace losses.

tobacco.title: Quit cigarettes and shisha
tobacco.intro: It is the step with the biggest effect on how Crohn's disease evolves. Here are four steps to get started.

date.title: Set a date
date.text: pick a calm day, for example early in the week, and prepare a few days before.

triggers.title: Spot risky moments
triggers.text: morning coffee, the work break, shisha with friends or the evening after iftar during Ramadan. Plan an alternative: walk, drink water, chew gum.

entourage.title: Tell the people around you
entourage.text: ask family and friends not to offer you cigarettes or shisha, and not to smoke near you.

help.title: Get support
help.text: your doctor or a smoking-cessation specialist can offer support and suitable nicotine replacement. Don't give up after a slip: start again.

community.subtitle: Talk with other patients
community.rules: You appear under your nickname, never your name. Be kind, don't share personal data and don't give treatment advice: only your doctor can do that.

pseudonym.title: Choose your nickname
pseudonym.explain: Your real name is never shown in the community. Choose a nickname that can't identify you.

pseudonym.invalid: This nickname contains characters that are not allowed.
